title: AI infrastructure: Scale advantages need not create monopoly
desc: Examines contested data moats, open models and make-or-buy dependence across infrastructure providers and legal firms.

kps.k: AI’s resource requirements may concentrate control over the technology underlying legal applications, but the evidence does not establish an inevitable monopoly.
kps.d: An Antimonopoly Approach to Governing Artificial Intelligence and On the Opportunities and Risks of Foundation Models argue that expensive compute, prepared data and infrastructure favour well-resourced developers. Generative AI at Work supplies the technical premise: model quality depends strongly on scale, alongside architectural and training advances. Cost figures remain reported estimates with different scopes: Generative AI at Work gives roughly $5 million in GPT-3 computing costs, while the antimonopoly account reports $10–12 million per training run; GPT-4 figures carry explicit uncertainty. AI Market Domination and the Natural Monopoly Problem predicts concentration among a few players but questions the stronger natural-monopoly analogy.

qs.q: Recent progress in generative AI has been driven by four factors: computing scale, earlier innovations in model architecture, the ability to “pre-train” using large amounts of unlabeled data and refinements in training techniques.8         First, the quality of LLMs is strongly dependent on scale: the amount of computing power used for training, the number of model parameters, and dataset size (Kaplan et al., 2020).
qs.a: Generative AI at Work · Academia · 2025

qs.q: Some reports have put the training of GPT-3 at $10-12       million for each training run.
qs.a: An Antimonopoly Approach to Governing Artificial Intelligence · Academia · 2024

kps.k: The durability of data advantages remains contested, with different mechanisms operating at the infrastructure and law-firm levels.
kps.d: The antimonopoly account identifies costly labelling, proprietary access and deployment feedback as barriers; models that learn from use may acquire reinforcing first-mover advantages. A View of How Language Models Will Transform Law instead tentatively predicts that exclusive legal-data advantages will weaken as work product circulates and lawyers move between firms. It distinguishes publicly filed litigation documents from agreements that can remain confidential. These positions need not conflict directly: diffusion of firm-specific expertise does not eliminate platform-level data or compute advantages. The legal account still expects capital-funded processing power to confer a temporary advantage.

qs.q: As noted, while some data is freely and easily available, it may require significant resources to transform and label.
qs.a: An Antimonopoly Approach to Governing Artificial Intelligence · Academia · 2024

qs.q: Attorney work product such as complaints and briefs become public more quickly than confidential agreements, which can be held privately for longer periods of time (and sometimes forever).
qs.a: A View of How Language Models Will Transform Law · Academia · 2024

kps.k: Open models can broaden downstream participation without necessarily decentralising infrastructure or ownership.
kps.d: Generative AI and the Courts presents the release it calls DeepSeq.AI as a potential challenge to dependence on large technology companies. Bridget McCormack cites Hugging Face’s report of 600 derivative models as evidence of rapid reuse, not proof of lasting market competition. On the Opportunities and Risks of Foundation Models acknowledges community initiatives but predicts a persistent resource gap. The antimonopoly account explains why these outcomes can coexist: open-model users may still depend on dominant clouds, restrictive licences and commercially motivated platform owners. A View of How Language Models Will Transform Law makes disruption conditional on inexpensive models matching proprietary capabilities.

qs.q: I listened to a lot of the commentary about it—much of it was confusing, with lots of numbers and debate about what really happened—but to me, the biggest takeaway is that this really could democratize AI development.
qs.a: Generative AI and the Courts: Expanding Legal Access or Opening the Floodgates? — full episode transcript · Regulators & courts · 2025

qs.q: Third, and relatedly, without a significant change in the industrial organization of those layers, any open-source AI foundation model will be dependent on an oligopoly of the biggest technology companies.
qs.a: An Antimonopoly Approach to Governing Artificial Intelligence · Academia · 2024

kps.k: Efficiency improvements and specialised models offer counterweights to scale barriers, but their competitive effects remain uncertain.
kps.d: A View of How Language Models Will Transform Law cites research on 470 GPU models released during 2006–2021 showing performance per dollar doubling every 2.5 years, while warning against assuming that trend will continue. It also identifies better document preparation, compression and task-focused distillation as cost-reduction routes; a cited 19.5-fold processing speed-up is a technical result, not a demonstrated saving across legal practice. Preventing Harm Amidst the AI Hype proposes smaller models for narrow legal and other uses and invokes DeepSeek as an illustration of alternative design constraints. Neither that discussion nor the courts episode establishes that reported lower development costs remove recurring computation requirements or infrastructure dependence.

kps.k: Legal providers face a make-or-buy trade-off between suppliers’ scale economies and dependence on upstream access terms.
kps.d: A View of How Language Models Will Transform Law argues theoretically that specialist model vendors can spread technical and data-management costs across law-firm customers, usually making internal development less attractive. It considers unique data, lower internal costs and firm consolidation as possible exceptions rather than observed purchasing patterns. Using an open model may avoid licensing fees without removing the cost of retrieving and synthesising legal documents. The antimonopoly account adds that vertical integration, cloud switching costs and model owners’ control over access can expose downstream developers to higher prices and weaker quality competition. Together, these arguments make recurring processing costs, access conditions and switching barriers relevant alongside initial development costs.

qs.q: Model Builder L very likely possesses a comparative advantage in model building and industry data management.
qs.a: A View of How Language Models Will Transform Law · Academia · 2024

qs.q: Nevertheless, they tend to stick with the higher-cost approach because of the costs and technical obstacles associated with switching.
qs.a: An Antimonopoly Approach to Governing Artificial Intelligence · Academia · 2024

kps.k: The policy tension concerns how to share scale efficiencies without allowing infrastructure owners to capture the benefits or restrict opportunity.
kps.d: AI Market Domination and the Natural Monopoly Problem argues conditionally that shared model infrastructure could reduce duplicated investment and carbon costs while preserving competition in applications. The antimonopoly account also acknowledges productive-efficiency benefits, but warns that power can extend across vertically integrated layers. On the Opportunities and Risks of Foundation Models broadens the concern to concentrated decision rights, income and social mobility for non-owners; it presents these as risks, not measured inevitable consequences. The practical policy implication is to examine hardware, cloud and access arrangements as well as model openness. The supplied material advocates public-interest, efficiency-conscious intervention without specifying a concrete regulatory mechanism.

qs.q: If we are more efficient at model building and we get competition in the application, well, that's good for us.
qs.a: AI Market Domination and the Natural Monopoly Problem · Academia · 2025

qs.q: This gives model developers significant power that they may leverage into adjacent layers of the AI stack.

vlens.an: The selected academia and research sources collectively accept the proposition’s core distinction: compute, prepared data, capital and infrastructure create strong concentration pressures, but they do not establish inevitable monopoly. They materially develop that proposition by identifying several mechanisms and counterweights. Concentration can arise through scale-dependent model quality, costly data preparation, deployment feedback, vertical integration, cloud switching barriers and model owners’ control of access terms. Conversely, legal work-product diffusion, lawyer mobility, cheaper hardware, model compression, specialist models and open development may weaken some advantages. The central internal variation concerns durability and policy. Some sources expect persistent oligopolistic infrastructure control and argue that open models cannot decentralise the underlying cloud and hardware layers; the legal-economic account is more tentative, predicting that firm-specific data advantages may wane and that lower-cost models could disrupt competition if they reach proprietary capability. Another source explores shared infrastructure as potentially efficient if application-level competition and public benefits are preserved. The technical workplace study supplies evidence that model performance is scale-dependent but does not itself infer market concentration, so its position remains unclear. Overall, these curated sources extend rather than merely repeat the proposition by separating model, infrastructure and legal-firm layers and by framing the outcome as conditional on technological cost trends, access arrangements and policy choices.

qs.q: And even if we're not confident that every one of these is a natural monopoly, I think we're pretty sure that all of these is some form of a natural oligopoly.
qs.a: AI Market Domination and the Natural Monopoly Problem · Academia · 2025

qs.q: One can conclude in sum, albeit somewhat tentatively, that competitive advantage based upon unique access to excellent data will wane as LLMs continue their ascent.
qs.a: A View of How Language Models Will Transform Law · Academia · 2024

vlens.an: The curated access-to-justice and civil-society source supports the proposition that AI’s scale advantages can restrict participation without making monopoly inevitable. Its principal reason is that prevailing AI development requires substantial energy, computing capacity, suitable infrastructure and data, making tool-building less accessible to less-resourced participants. At the same time, it identifies smaller, use-case-specific models and altered design constraints as possible counterweights. The source’s internal qualification is material but does not make its position mixed: these alternatives are presented as possibilities, illustrated partly through DeepSeek, rather than as demonstrated evidence that infrastructure dependence or concentration has been overcome. Because only one source from this professional voice is supplied, no broader prevalence or consensus within the group can be inferred.

qs.q: That said, the overwhelming majority of ways that people are creating them is very power intensive and very reliant on large amounts of data, large amounts of power, which does make it a bit less accessible for a wide variety of people to sort of play and develop tools in this space.

vlens.an: This professional voice supports the cluster’s principal proposition that scale advantages may concentrate AI infrastructure without making monopoly inevitable. The episode treats the open-source release as a plausible counterweight to dependence on large technology companies: reported competitive performance and lower resource requirements suggest that challengers may be able to enter, while rapid downstream reuse provides concrete evidence that access to model development broadened in the immediate aftermath. Its claims remain appropriately bounded. The speakers describe democratisation, stronger competition and startup formation as potential or expected outcomes, not as proof that infrastructure concentration, recurring compute costs or dependence on dominant cloud providers has disappeared. Internal variation is limited but material: the opening speaker advances the wider competitive forecast despite acknowledging disputed and confusing reporting, whereas Bridget McCormack adds a specific short-term indicator—600 derivative models reportedly created within four days. As this is one curated source with multiple speakers, it establishes a supportive perspective within this professional voice, not the prevalence of that view among regulators, courts or professional bodies generally.

qs.q: I listened to a lot of the commentary about it—much of it was confusing, with lots of numbers and debate about what really happened—but to me, the biggest takeaway is that this really could democratize AI development.

elens.an: The 2015–2022 source supports the proposition that foundation-model scale advantages can concentrate control without making monopoly inevitable. It attributes centralization to the resource intensity of frontier development and to large technology companies’ advantages in infrastructure, users and data. It also identifies material consequences beyond market structure, including concentrated decision rights and reduced opportunities for non-owners. At the same time, its account is qualified rather than deterministic: grassroots open-source and distributed-training initiatives are presented as counterweights, although the source predicts that substantial data and compute requirements will probably preserve or widen the capability gap between private and community-accessible models. The evidence supplied is primarily qualitative reasoning, examples and predictions, not a quantified demonstration of monopoly or its inevitability. Because this facet contains one curated source, it establishes that source’s position rather than the prevalence of the view during the period.

qs.q: As a result, the ownership of data and models are often highly centralized, leading to market concentration (§5.6: ethics).
qs.a: On the Opportunities and Risks of Foundation Models · Academia · 2021

qs.q: To counterbalance this centralization, there have been grassroots efforts to open source AI research such as Masakhane, EleutherAI, and HuggingFace, or build foundation models through distributed training.
qs.a: On the Opportunities and Risks of Foundation Models · Academia · 2021

elens.an: The 2023–2024 sources accept the principal proposition that AI’s capital, compute and data requirements create substantial concentration pressures without making monopoly inevitable, and they materially develop it by distinguishing different layers and mechanisms. Both emphasise costly compute, prepared data and supplier scale economies. The antimonopoly account stresses potentially durable platform-level concentration through vertical integration, deployment-data feedback, cloud dependence and switching costs; even open models may remain reliant on a small group of infrastructure providers. The legal-sector account is more qualified about durable firm-level moats: it predicts that proprietary legal knowledge may diffuse through public work product and lawyer mobility, while capital-funded processing power provides only a temporary advantage. It further adds a make-or-buy analysis in which specialist model suppliers can spread development and data-management costs across customers, although legal providers then face recurring processing costs and dependence on upstream access terms. Thus, the internal variation concerns where concentration persists and how durable it is—not whether scale advantages exist. These curated sources should not be treated as representative of all commentary from the period.

qs.q: PROCESSING POWER AND FIRM ORGANIZATION      Even if legal data is difficult to hoard, competitive advantage will be acquired, and for a while maintained, through access to processing power made possible through capital investment.
qs.a: A View of How Language Models Will Transform Law · Academia · 2024

qs.q: Third, and relatedly, without a significant change in the industrial organization of those layers, any open-source AI foundation model will be dependent on an oligopoly of the biggest technology companies.

elens.an: The selected 2025 sources support the synthesis’s principal proposition that resource and scale advantages can concentrate AI development without making monopoly inevitable. Their common reasoning is that compute, energy, data and infrastructure requirements restrict participation and favour well-resourced developers, while open releases, rapid downstream reuse, specialised models and alternative design constraints may broaden development. Material variation concerns the likely market structure and the strength of these counterweights: one source predicts oligopoly rather than natural monopoly and argues that concentrated model infrastructure could yield efficiency and environmental benefits if application-layer competition and public-interest policy are preserved; another treats open-source reuse as promising evidence of wider participation but not proof of durable competition; a third presents smaller, targeted models as possible rather than demonstrated solutions. The technical source establishes scale dependence and rising resource commitments but does not itself draw conclusions about concentration. Overall, the period’s evidence aligns with the synthesis’s qualified balance rather than establishing either inevitable monopoly or successful decentralisation.
